13.5 Solutions to Exercises 5 - Exercises on homomorphisms, isomorphisms and quotient groups Solution. (Question 5.4.1) (a) Everything in C7 is a power of the cycle ρ = (1 2 3 4 5 6 7). So for all ρ n, ρ m ∈ C7 we have φ(ρnρm) = (ρ nρm) 2 = ρ nρmρnρm = ρ 2nρ2m = φ(ρ n)φ(ρm). So, this is a homomorphism. Be careful — we really used the fact that C7 is abelian here. Is it an isomorphism? It’s certainly onto since you can easily check that: Im(φ) = {ρ 2×1, ρ 2×2, . . . , ρ2×7} = C7. One-to-one is slightly tricker: φ(ρn) = φ(ρ m) ⟹ ρ 2n = ρ2m ⟹ ρ 2(n−m) = e ⟹ 2(n − m)∣7 ⟹ (n − m)∣7 ⟹ ρn−m = e ⟹ ρn = ρ m. (b) We might think this is a homomorphism at first glance, but when you test it carefully things start to go wrong: φ(gh) = (gh)2 = ghgh but φ(g)φ(h) = g2h2. Because S7 is not abelian, it’s not true in general that ghgh = g2h2. All we need to do is find some elements confirming this! Let g = (1 2 3) and h = (1 2). Then g2h2 = (1 3 2), while on the other hand ghgh = (1 2 3)(1 2)(1 2 3)(1 2) = (1)(2)(3) = e. So, for this pair, φ(gh) /= φ(g)φ(h). Hence φ is not a homomorphism. Thus certainly not an isomorphism. Solution. (Question 5.4.2) For any g ∈ G we have θ(g) = θ(eGg) = θ(eG)θ(g). Right multiplying both sides by (θ(g))−1 we have, θ(g) (θ(g))−1 = θ(eG)θ(g) (θ(g)) −1 . Hence eH = θ(eG)eH . Therefore eH = θ(eG). Solution. (Question 5.4.3) We will handle the m ∈ N case first. Fix g ∈ G and m ∈ N. Then θ(gm) = θ(gm−1)θ(g) = θ(gm−2)θ(g)θ(g) = ⋯ = θ(g)⋯θ(g)θ(g) (m times) = θ(g)m. [You could also easily prove this by induction.] Solution. (Question 5.4.4) Let K = Ker(θ). Fix a, b ∈ K and note that θ(a) = θ(b) = eG by definition. Now fix g ∈ G. For all a ∈ K we have θ(g−1ag) = (θ(g))−1θ(a)θ(g) = (θ(g))−1eGθ(g) = eG. Hence g−1ag ∈ K for all a ∈ K. Hence, K ⊴ G. [Optional: To prove K is a subgroup, use the Quick Subgroup Test. Firstly, we have already shown θ(eG) = eH , therefore eG ∈ K. Secondly, θ(ab) = θ(a)θ(b) = eGeG = eG, so ab ∈ K. Thirdly, θ(a −1) = (θ(a))−1 = e −1 G = eG, so a −1 ∈ K. Hence, by the Quick Subgroup Test, K ≤ G.]

Solution. (Question 5.4.5) Write out all the elements of D6 and all the elements of S3: D6 = {e, ρ, ρ 2, σ, σρ, σρ2} with ρσ = σρ−1, and σ2 = e, and ρ3 = e. S3 = {e, (1 2 3), (1 3 2), (1 2), (1 3), (2 3)}. Now let θ ∶ D6 → S3 be the map given by θ(ρ) = (1 2 3) and θ(σ) = (1 2). Then let: θ(e) = e θ(ρ 2) = θ(ρ)θ(ρ) = (1 2 3)2 = (1 3 2) θ(σρ) = θ(σ)θ(ρ) = (1 2)(1 2 3) = (2 3) θ(σρ2) = θ(σ)θ(ρ 2) = (1 2)(1 3 2) = (1 3) We can now easily check that θ is well-defined and is a homomorphism. You can also easily see that it is one- to-one (all images are different) and onto (everything is S3 lies in the image). Hence this is an isomorphism.
